strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 36 MMEB datasets and multiple benchmarks with systematic ablation studies (Table 3) demonstrating each component's contribution

Well-motivated empirical insights: probing experiments (Fig. 2) clearly demonstrate semantic collapse after final MLP layer (94% → 87% similarity), providing solid motivation for the lexicalization pressure hypothesis
Novel discovery of LLM framing effect showing logically equivalent label formats yield divergent accuracies (8.4% gap between True/False and Right/Wrong), with elegant MCQ-based solution
Strong practical results: outperforming models trained on millions of pairs (GME-7B on 8M pairs, MMRet-7B on 26.2M pairs) without any training data
Generalization across diverse MLLM families and scales (Qwen, LLaVA, InternVL; 2B-32B parameters) with consistent improvements, demonstrating broad applicability
Good experimental practices: error analysis (Appendix G), cross-lingual evaluation (Table 7), and evaluation on multiple standard benchmarks (Flickr30K, COCO) beyond primary benchmark
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of individual contributions: removing the final MLP is a straightforward architectural choice, controlled prompting extends existing work (PromptEOL, MetaEOL) incrementally, and MCQ framing is relatively basic prompt engineering rather than methodological innovation

Weak theoretical justification: Lemma C.1 merely restates that language modeling projects representations onto vocabulary subspace (well-known property) without rigorously explaining why this specifically harms retrieval or connecting the 7% semantic similarity drop to the 13.9% performance gain over E5-V

Misleading 'training-free' framing: method relies on extensive task-specific prompt engineering with three carefully designed constraints; sensitivity analysis is minimal (Table 3b only shows progressive constraint addition, not prompt variations), raising questions whether this constitutes a form of hidden tuning

Unfair comparisons with training-based methods: frequently compares zero-shot FreeRet against methods trained on MMEB (e.g., UniME-V2), presenting this as if training is unnecessary rather than acknowledging fundamentally different experimental settings; only E5-V reproduced as zero-shot baseline

Unresolved computational efficiency concerns: acknowledges higher latency than CLIP but relegates solutions to appendix; proposed mitigations (lightweight pre-filtering, controlled reranking) essentially reintroduce two-stage pipelines and undermine 'unified retriever' narrative

Overstated claims: 'state-of-the-art' repeatedly used despite comparing zero-shot against supervised baselines; Figure 1(c) comparison visually misleading regarding alignment with MMEB-supervised methods; framing narrative suggests training is unnecessary rather than acknowledging different optimization settings

Insufficient analysis of design choices: (1) MCQ framing effect only measured on ImageNet-1K classification—does 8.4% improvement generalize across all 36 datasets?; (2) Table 3a shows 5.7% improvement from removing final MLP but doesn't explain why h^MLP_{L-2} removal hurts performance; (3) no systematic prompt sensitivity study despite claim of being prompt-driven

Reproducibility gaps: exact prompt templates for all task types not fully specified, no details on how constraints are instantiated per benchmark task, promise of code release doesn't address current implementation clarity issues

Limited zero-shot baseline comparisons and missing analysis: only E5-V reproduced; no comparisons with other training-free methods (PromptEOL, MetaEOL, TokenPrepend, Echo-Embedding); framing effect analysis is shallow—why MCQ specifically works beyond vague 'neutrality' claims; why does larger model show higher framing sensitivity (7B vs. 3B)

strengths: Well-motivated and rigorously validated insights: Lexicalization pressure analysis is compelling with clear probing experiments across multiple model scales showing 7% semantic similarity drop. LLM framing effect is novel and practically significant (5% accuracy difference).

Comprehensive experimental validation: Tested on 36 MMEB datasets, multiple MLLM families/scales (Qwen/InternVL/LLaVA, 2B-32B), cross-lingual performance (EN/ZH/FR), and standard benchmarks (Flickr30K, COCO) with clear ablations quantifying each component's contribution.

Strong empirical results: FreeRet-2B outperforms GME-7B (trained on 8M pairs) and MMRet-7B (26.2M pairs); FreeRet-7B matches MMEB-supervised methods; video subset shows even larger improvements (63.2% vs 39.3%).

Practical value and immediate deployment: True plug-and-play with any MLLM variant, preserves generative abilities, supports arbitrary modality combinations (addressing the 15×15=225 pair scalability bottleneck), eliminates expensive fine-tuning cycles.

Thorough analytical depth: Semantic analysis using cross-lingual synonym/antonym pairs provides strong evidence of lexicalization effects; honest error analysis identifies failure modes; computational efficiency analysis clarifies overhead vs. separate-model approaches.

Rigorous experimental methodology: Clear ablations isolate component contributions, cross-lingual validation despite translation artifacts, computational analysis with flexible efficiency-accuracy trade-offs (Table 10), reproducibility details with promised code.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of individual components: Removing final MLP is straightforward; prompt engineering for LLM improvements is explored in prior work (PromptEOL, MetaEOL); MCQ formatting for LLMs is not entirely new. Main novelty is in combination rather than conceptual innovation.

Significant computational efficiency concerns: Reranking top-50 candidates requires ~3s latency on 7B model (Table 10), orders of magnitude slower than CLIP-based methods. For 100M+ candidate scenarios, proposed solutions (pre-filtering, controlled reranking, lightweight MLLMs) are standard techniques rather than innovations.

Theoretical understanding gaps: Appendix C provides only basic linear algebra argument without explaining why semantic fidelity improves retrieval specifically. The 7% semantic similarity drop may have alternative explanations not thoroughly explored. Connection between lexicalization pressure and retrieval performance lacks formal rigor.

Prompt engineering dependency undermines training-free claim: Carefully crafted prompts (semantic grounding, noise suppression, task alignment) represent domain-specific engineering. Sensitivity to prompt variations not analyzed; unclear whether prompts are MMEB-optimized or generalizable; contradicts 'no training' narrative.

Substantial performance variation across settings: 15% spread across model families (InternVL3-2B: 58.5% vs Qwen2.5-VL-32B: 73.3%); cross-lingual drops significantly (67.8%→60.4%); raises questions about universality of effectiveness and whether gains are primarily from larger models.

Evaluation scope limitations: Precision@1 is strict metric; Recall@5/10 results missing. MMEB weights image/text heavily; video/audio underrepresented. Omni-modal experiments purely qualitative (2 examples). No evaluation on specialized domains (medical/legal/scientific) where generalization is unclear.

Incomplete analysis of design choices: Why does framing effect sensitivity increase with model scale? Section 3.4 hypothesis stated but not rigorously investigated. Limited discussion of when training-free retrieval would fail or why success is specific to MMEB vs generalizable.

Benchmark comparison concerns: Mixing supervised/unsupervised methods in Table 1 could be clearer; some baselines' training data specifications ambiguous; E5-V labeled 'training-free' but was pretrained; limited out-of-distribution generalization testing beyond 3 standard benchmarks.
